Lessons.Title: Represent Numbers in Different Ways
ExplanationParagraphs: Represent Numbers in Different Ways: the same whole can be shown as a numeral, a number name, base-ten blocks or a diagram, and a sum. A hundred has the same value as ten tens, and a ten has the same value as ten ones. Exchanging these units changes the representation while preserving the whole. Use blocks if they help you explain.

Warm-up — Which One Doesn’t Belong? Compare A, a diagram with 3 hundreds and 7 tens; B, 300 + 70 + 1; C, 300 + 60 + 10; and D, 400 − 30. Think quietly, choose one and explain your reason to a partner. A, C and D each represent 370, while B represents 371. B can be singled out by value, A by being a diagram, D by subtraction, or C by its particular non-standard sum; a sound reason matters more than choosing one preferred letter. Explain the vocabulary you use.

Expanded form has a precise meaning: write the value of each digit in its place. For 482, standard expanded form is 400 + 80 + 2. Other decompositions can be correct without being standard expanded form. For example, 100 + 60 + 15 equals 175, but the 15 contains a ten and five ones; the standard expanded form of 175 is 100 + 70 + 5.

Card Sort: Numbers in Their Different Forms — work in pairs with the twelve cards A–L. The independently drawn cards in the companion preserve the original mathematical information. Match every numeral, number name, diagram or sum that names the same whole. Take turns explaining, using “I noticed …, so I matched …”, and ask for clarification when you disagree (MLR8). Begin with a smaller subset if helpful, then add the remaining cards. Use place-value terminology and blocks to justify matches.

The complete matching groups are A–G–L for 175, B–H for 813, C–F for 371, D–I–J for 299, and E–K for 329. Card C has 3 hundreds, 7 tens and 1 one. Card J has 2 hundreds, 9 tens and 9 ones. Do not force every group to contain the same number of cards. Record the matches and explain why each representation has the same value; the teacher checks the sort and reasoning.

Numbers in Different Forms Round Table: first discuss decompositions of 365. Examples include 300 + 60 + 5, 200 + 160 + 5, and 300 + 50 + 15. Work in groups of four. Each pupil writes an original three-digit number in Box 1. Pass the paper to the right and receive from the left; write a decomposition in Box 2. Pause for instructions. Pass again, then put a different decomposition in Box 3. Pass again and fill Box 4 differently from both earlier decompositions. One more pass returns the paper to its original writer. Each decomposition must preserve the number in Box 1, rather than replacing it with a new number.

Discuss which box was hardest and what helped. Independently write connections among the decompositions on your own sheet, then compare everyone’s sheets for patterns. For 365, exchanging one hundred for ten tens changes 3 hundreds, 6 tens and 5 ones into 2 hundreds, 16 tens and 5 ones. Exchanging one ten for ten ones gives 3 hundreds, 5 tens and 15 ones. Distinct place-value groupings can represent the same whole. The teacher reviews the different boxes, original choices and actual group exchange; a numeric total cannot certify those activities.

Lesson synthesis: decompose 253 as 200 + 50 + 3, 200 + 40 + 13, or 100 + 150 + 3. For 253 + 134, explain why grouping hundreds with hundreds, tens with tens and ones with ones may be useful: 300 + 80 + 7 = 387. This is preparation for later place-value addition, not a demand for a new formal algorithm today. Compare strategies and make space for everyone’s ideas.

Independent practice uses a fresh numeral-to-sum conversion. For a separate worked exchange, 624 can be represented by 6 hundreds, 2 tens and 4 ones, or 5 hundreds, 12 tens and 4 ones. Check the total value after any exchange. A whole-number triple entered in hundreds,tens,ones order can have more than nine tens or ones; those are intentional non-standard decompositions, not automatically mistakes.

New Edulytics Cool-down: represent 572 with counts of hundreds, tens and ones. Enter one valid grouping, then show at least two different decompositions and explain an exchange that preserves the whole. Use numerals, a word name, an expanded sum or blocks to connect the forms. The numerical checker validates one grouping only; your teacher reviews the other forms, distinctness and explanation. The publisher-gated Let Me Count the Ways prompt was not read or reproduced.

Optional centers: Target Numbers, stage 6, begins with a three-cube starting number shared by both partners. On each turn roll three cubes, choose whether each roll contributes hundreds, tens or ones, and write the new sum. Play six rounds, using the previous sum as the next starting value; closest to 1,000 without going over wins. Five in a Row: Addition and Subtraction, stage 8, uses two clips to select addends, adds their values and covers the sum. Partners alternate moving one clip; the first to cover five in a row wins. Original optional sheets are linked for teacher-led play; no publisher gameboard artwork is embedded.

KeyConcepts.Title: Place-value units
KeyConcepts.Definition: Hundreds, tens and ones have different values.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Multiply each count by its unit value, then add.

KeyConcepts.Title: Standard expanded form
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each term is the value of one digit in its position.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Separate hundreds, tens and ones by digit value.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent decompositions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different groupings can represent the same number.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Exchange 1 hundred for 10 tens or 1 ten for 10 ones without changing total.

KeyConcepts.Title: Match forms by value
KeyConcepts.Definition: A numeral, number name, sum or diagram can name the same whole.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Read every place-value part; do not match only by appearance.
KeyConcepts.Example: Two hundred ninety-nine matches 299 and a diagram of 2 hundreds 9 tens 9 ones.

WorkedExamples.Title: A sum that is not standard expanded form
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the value of 300+60+10.
WorkedExamples.Method: Combine the tens before reading the numeral.
Steps: The numeral is 370 and standard expanded form can be written 300+70.
WorkedExamples.Check: The warm-up diagram of 3 hundreds 7 tens gives the same value.

WorkedExamples.Title: Connect a word name and diagram
WorkedExamples.Question: Why do cardsD,I,J match?
WorkedExamples.Check: Distinguish cardJ from cardC, which has 3 hundreds 7 tens 1 one.

WorkedExamples.Title: A new exchange example
WorkedExamples.Question: Represent 624 in two different place-value groupings.
WorkedExamples.Method: Trade one hundred for ten tens.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 6,2,4 and 5,12,4 are different valid hundreds,tens,ones groupings.
WorkedExamples.Check: The counts differ but the total value is unchanged.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling every sum a standard expanded form.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A sum such as 100+60+15 includes a two-digit ones term and is a non-standard decomposition.
CommonMistakes.Correction: It still equals 175; standard expanded form is 100+70+5.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Rejecting more than nine tens or ones in every representation.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Exchanges deliberately create equivalent non-standard groupings.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check the weighted total rather than requiring one preferred grouping.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Matching cards by one similar digit or requiring groups of equal size.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source deck has both pairs and triples, and forms must agree in value.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use all five complete groups and justify each part.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Changing the original number while passing the round-table sheet.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Each later box must represent the same Box 1 whole in a different way.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Read the original number and earlier decompositions before adding a new one.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a correct scalar as the whole task.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Card matches, number names, diagrams, distinct decompositions and partner exchanges need evidence.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Show the representations and explain them for teacher review.

SummaryPoints: Match numerals, names, diagrams and sums by the whole they represent.
Standard expanded form lists each digit’s place value.
A hundred can be exchanged for ten tens; a ten for ten ones.
Different valid decompositions can have more than nine tens or ones.
The twelve source cards form five groups, including both pairs and triples.
Keep the same original three-digit number throughout the four-box round table.
Teacher reviews matching explanations, different decompositions, patterns and actual group work.
